name: Personality Trait Validity

nodeContents.query: What do Big Five traits actually predict?
nodeContents.response:
## The short version

Effects are real and mostly replicate, but they live in the $r = 0.1$–$0.3$ band. The best benchmark study here is Soto's LOOPR project: ([How Replicable Are Links Between Personality Traits and Consequential Life Outcomes? The Life Outcomes of Personality Replication Project - Christopher J. Soto, 2019](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0956797619831612)) preregistered, high-powered replications (median N = 1,504) of 78 published trait–outcome associations, of which 87% were significant in the expected direction, with replication effects typically 77% as strong as the originals. So: a mostly honest literature, with effect sizes inflated maybe 25% by publication bias and researcher degrees of freedom.

## Where the signal actually is

| Outcome | Main trait | Rough magnitude |
|---|---|---|
| Life satisfaction / subjective well-being | Neuroticism (−), Extraversion (+) | $r \approx .3$–.5 — the largest in the field |
| Internalizing disorders (depression, anxiety) | Neuroticism | $r \approx .4+$; arguably the same construct measured twice |
| Job performance | Conscientiousness | operational $r \approx .19$ decontextualized, ~.25 for "at work" measures |
| Academic grades | Conscientiousness | $r \approx .2$, roughly IQ-sized at university level |
| Longevity / mortality | Conscientiousness | $r \approx .1$, robust across cohorts |
| Divorce, relationship dissolution | Neuroticism (+), Agreeableness (−) | $r \approx .2$ |
| Political ideology | Openness (liberal), Conscientiousness (conservative) | $r \approx .2$ |
| Income | Conscientiousness (+), Agreeableness (−) | $r \approx .1$–.2 |

Two structural facts worth holding onto. First, the workhorses are Conscientiousness and Neuroticism; Openness and Agreeableness predict tastes and relationships more than achievement. Second, the field's estimates keep shrinking under better methods — ([Revisiting the design of selection systems in light of new findings regarding the validity of widely used predictors | Industrial and Organizational Psychology | Cambridge Core](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/industrial-and-organizational-psychology/article/revisiting-the-design-of-selection-systems-in-light-of-new-findings-regarding-the-validity-of-widely-used-predictors/A20984B138319E3D432E643978BF026D)) Sackett et al. (2022) found flaws in range-restriction corrections in prior selection meta-analyses and produced revised, often substantially lower, validity estimates.

The obvious next fork: whether $r = .2$ is impressive or trivial (it depends entirely on whether you're picking one person or a population), or whether these correlations survive when predictor and outcome aren't both self-reported.

nodeContents.query: Is a correlation of .3 big or small?
nodeContents.response:
## Two different questions hide in this one

**If you're predicting one person**, $r = .3$ is nearly worthless. Knowing someone's Conscientiousness leaves the residual SD of the outcome at $\sqrt{1-r^2} = 0.954$ — you have narrowed your uncertainty by **4.6%**. That is the honest answer to "should I use a personality test to decide about this individual?" (Squaring $r$ into "9% of variance" is the classic way to make this sound even worse than it is; ([Evaluating Effect Size in Psychological Research](https://www2.psych.ubc.ca/~schaller/528Readings/FunderOzer2019.pdf)) Funder and Ozer flag squaring effect-size $r$s as one of the two most common misinterpretations.)

**If you're sorting a population**, the same number is powerful. With bivariate normal data and $r = .3$:

| Group | Chance of landing in the top decile of the outcome |
|---|---|
| Top decile on the trait | ~22% |
| Base rate | 10% |
| Bottom decile on the trait | ~3% |

A 7:1 ratio between the tails, from a correlation you cannot see in any single case. This is why $r = .2$ is simultaneously useless for hiring *this* candidate and valuable for a firm making 10,000 hires.

## Where .3 sits in the field ([Effect size guidelines for individual differences researchers - ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0191886916308194))

Gignac and Szodorai collated 708 meta-analytic correlations from individual-differences research; the 25th, 50th and 75th percentiles were .10, .20 and .30. So $r=.3$ is the *75th percentile of everything the field has ever found* — ([2 Benchmarks – Guide to Effect Sizes and Confidence Intervals](https://matthewbjane.quarto.pub/Benchmarks.html)) on Funder and Ozer's revised guidelines it counts as a large effect, potentially powerful in both the short and long run, while ([Automated Interpretation of Indices of Effect Size • effectsize](https://easystats.github.io/effectsize/articles/interpret.html)) $r \geq .40$ is likely "a gross overestimate that will rarely be found in a large sample or in a replication."

The irony: .30 was originally the *indictment*. Mischel's 1968 critique named it the "personality coefficient" — the ceiling that supposedly proved traits didn't exist. The number didn't move; the interpretation did, once people noticed that situations and clinical interventions don't beat it either.

The live question is therefore not the size but the source: does .3 survive when the outcome isn't self-reported?

nodeContents.query: Do traits change over a lifetime?
nodeContents.response:
## Two different questions hide in "change"

**Rank-order** (does your position in the distribution hold?) and **mean-level** (does the whole cohort drift?). They have opposite-feeling answers.

**Rank order rises but never locks.** Roberts & DelVecchio's meta-analysis of 152 longitudinal studies found test–retest consistency climbing with age: ([The rank-order consistency of personality traits from childhood to old age: a quantitative review of longitudinal studies - PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/10668348/)) ~.31 in childhood, .54 in the college years, .64 at 30, plateauing near .74 between 50 and 70 — all at a fixed 6.7-year interval. The sharper fact is what happens to long lags: stability doesn't just decay slowly, it ([(PDF) Personality Stability and Change: A Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Studies](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/362021332_Personality_stability_and_change_A_meta-analysis_of_longitudinal_studies)) declines fast at first, then attenuates and appears to plateau at modest values around $r \approx .20$. So the correlation between you-at-20 and you-at-60 is roughly the size of the trait–outcome effects in [1] — worth holding against [[da5b6eb6-a868-432f-95e7-3ec8e111137b]].

**Mean levels move in one direction.** The maturity principle: ([\[PDF\] The rank-order consistency of personality traits from childhood to old age: a quantitative review of longitudinal studies. | Semantic Scholar](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/The-rank-order-consistency-of-personality-traits-to-Roberts-DelVecchio/bb8a2b002b961a97780d97bb04c7a6e04c3c6add)) people rise on conscientiousness, emotional stability and social dominance in young adulthood, and decline on openness (and social vitality) later. Cumulatively this is on the order of half a SD to a full SD across adulthood — larger than almost any single trait–outcome correlation.

**Deliberate change is faster than development.** Roberts' meta-analysis of ([A Systematic Review of Personality Trait Change Through Intervention](https://www.ovid.com/journals/plbul/fulltext/10.1037/bul0000088~a-systematic-review-of-personality-trait-change-through)) 207 intervention studies found trait change of about $d = .37$ over an average of 24 weeks, concentrated in ([Differential Effects of Psychological Interventions in Online and Face-to-Face Settings on DSM-5 and ICD-11 Maladaptive Trait Domains: An Exploratory Pilot Study - PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8236509/)) neuroticism and (low) extraversion, with much of it achieved within 8 weeks — ([Changing personality traits with the help of a digital ...](https://www.pnas.org/doi/pdf/10.1073/pnas.2017548118)) most change lands in the first weeks and plateaus at 8–10. Volitional change (apps, if–then plans) works too, but ([A systematic review of volitional personality change research | Communications Psychology](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44271-024-00167-5)) merely having a change goal is only weakly related to actually changing.

The obvious skeptical fork: how much of that 24-week $d=.37$ is *trait* change versus mood-congruent self-report — a depressed patient rating "I worry a lot" differently after therapy. Same identification problem as the self-report confound flagged at the end of [1].

nodeContents.response:
## Not a rival model — a lossy re-encoding

MBTI's four axes are four of the Big Five, dichotomized. The classic convergences: ([Top-Down Influence? Predicting CEO Personality and Risk Impact from Speech Transcripts](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2201.07670)) introversion with extraversion at $r = -0.74$, intuition with openness at $0.72$, feeling with agreeableness at $0.44$, and perceiving with conscientiousness at $-0.49$. So the parts of MBTI that work are Big Five variance wearing Jungian labels; the parts that are distinctively Jungian — type dynamics, dominant/auxiliary function stacks — are the parts with essentially no empirical support.

Two specific losses:

**Neuroticism is simply absent.** Look back at the table in [1]: the largest effects in the field — life satisfaction, internalizing disorders — are Neuroticism effects. ([Personality Tests Aren’t All the Same. Some Work Better Than Others | Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/personality-tests-arent-all-the-same-some-work-better-than-others/)) MBTI-style tests typically don't measure neuroticism, which predicts outcomes like career success, suicidal ideation and life satisfaction. You've deleted the most predictive column.

**Dichotomizing a continuum.** Median-splitting a normally distributed score attenuates correlations by roughly $\sqrt{2/\pi} \approx 0.8$ and throws away information about everyone near the middle — which is most people, since the scores aren't bimodal. This is the real source of the famous instability: ([MBTI Criticisms: Valid Concerns and Unfair Attacks](https://www.earlyyears.tv/mbti-framework-critical-analysis/)) between 39% and 76% of test-takers get a different four-letter type when retested after as little as five weeks, even though ([MBTI Facts | The Myers-Briggs Company](https://ap.themyersbriggs.com/themyersbriggs-mbti-facts.aspx)) the underlying scales have internal consistencies around .90 and test-retest correlations over .80 out to 15 weeks. Decent scales, catastrophic categories.

**Head-to-head:** in a recent comparison across 37 life outcomes, the Big Five was about twice as accurate as an MBTI-style test, and adding MBTI results to Big Five ones produced no improvement — zero incremental validity.

The live question isn't MBTI specifically but whether *any* categorical model is defensible — whether personality types exist as replicable clusters rather than as splits imposed on continua.

nodeContents.query: Why do effect sizes shrink on replication?
nodeContents.response:
## Nothing decays — the published number was never an unbiased estimate

The dominant mechanism is a selection filter. Suppose the true correlation is $\rho = .20$ and the original study had $N = 50$: $SE \approx .14$, so significance requires an observed $r \ge .27$. Conditional on clearing that bar, the *expected* published $r$ is about **.36** — 80% inflation, with no dishonesty anywhere in the chain. At $N = 300$ the same filter inflates by ~3%. This is Gelman & Carlin's **Type M (magnitude) error**: the exaggeration ratio is essentially a function of power alone, and it is invisible from inside any single paper.

Three contributors stack on top of it:

- **Forking paths.** Every unreported covariate set, outcome variant or subgroup split multiplies the effective number of tests, which sharpens the same significance filter without appearing in the p-value.
- **Estimand drift.** Replications use different populations, shorter scales (lower reliability → attenuation) and different variance in the predictor. That's continuous with the range-restriction problem Sackett et al. exposed in [[a445518b-c46c-48b9-afe6-11ae6fd6225f]] — not bias, just a different quantity.
- **Selection of what gets replicated.** Studies are chosen for replication because they're notable, i.e. because their estimates were extreme.

## Why personality shrank less than the rest of psychology

The Open Science Collaboration's 2015 replications of social/cognitive psychology saw mean $r$ fall from ~.40 to ~.20 — roughly half. LOOPR's 77% retention is the field's good news, and it follows mechanically from the first point: personality findings typically came from large archival panels rather than $N = 40$ lab manipulations, so the winner's curse had less room to operate. Robust designs, not virtuous researchers.

**Practical rule:** apply a shrinkage prior of ~0.75 to a published personality $r$, harsher (0.5 or worse) when $N$ is small, the finding is surprising, or the result is an interaction. That's usually the difference between the "large effect" band and the median finding in [[da5b6eb6-a868-432f-95e7-3ec8e111137b]].

brief: I want to understand personality psychology better. The Big Five keeps being called “the scientific one” — what do its traits actually predict, how big are those effects really, and how well have they been replicated? I already know the pop typologies are weak, so don't spend my time debunking horoscopes.

suggestions.text: What does an effect of r = .2 imply for individual prediction versus population-level decisions?
How much do Big Five associations shrink when traits and outcomes are measured independently rather than by the same self-report method?
How much predictive value do Big Five traits add beyond IQ, demographics, and prior behavior?
How much of the apparent personality change after therapy survives informant reports, behavioral measures, and controls for symptom improvement?
When people deliberately change a trait, do the outcomes associated with that trait—such as grades, relationships, or well-being—change accordingly?
How confidently can longitudinal studies separate genuine age-related maturation from cohort effects and selective attrition?
How sensitive is the claimed 7:1 tail ratio to the assumptions of normality, reliable measurement, and a linear trait–outcome relationship?
For a real selection decision, how do the base rate, selection rate, and costs of false positives determine whether an r = .3 predictor is useful?
Is calling r = .3 “nearly worthless” for individual prediction statistically justified, or does the residual-SD framing understate meaningful probability updates?
Do personality data contain any replicable clusters that justify genuine “types,” or are the major traits continuously distributed?
How strong is the evidence that MBTI adds zero predictive validity beyond the Big Five, and has that head-to-head result replicated?
If MBTI’s underlying scales are reasonably reliable, could using its continuous scores retain useful predictive value despite the failure of four-letter categories?
How well supported is the proposed 0.75 shrinkage rule, and how should I adjust it using a study’s sample size, power, and analytic flexibility?
How can replication studies distinguish winner’s-curse inflation from genuine effect heterogeneity across populations and measurement instruments?
Do preregistered, highly powered Big Five studies still shrink in later replications, or does the replication gap largely disappear under those conditions?
What evidence would distinguish Big Five traits as causal dispositions from mere summaries of past behavior or shared causes that happen to predict future outcomes?
How much predictive value survives when personality tests face real applicants who can fake, coach, adapt, and learn what institutions reward?
Why do employers and institutions keep buying personality tests despite weak individual prediction—what functions besides prediction are those tests serving?
How well do trait–outcome correlations transport across countries and historical periods, and which institutions determine whether a trait like conscientiousness actually pays?
What is the theoretical ceiling on predicting decades-later outcomes from one Big Five measurement once test unreliability and lifetime personality change are included?
